turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Afternoon, Keagan. Have a seat. Your file says you're twenty-four — what brought you in today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. Um, my girlfriend made the booking, hey. She thinks something's up. I reckon it's nothing, honestly.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright. What is she noticing?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): My heart goes fast, like thumping, especially at night when I'm trying to sleep. She says I look stressed. I'm not.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has that racing been happening?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I can't give you a date. Sometime in the last couple of months. Maybe six weeks, maybe longer. I didn't write it down.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): When it comes, is it a flutter, a hard pound, or does it skip?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Sort of all of it — it skips and then it hammers. Not every day. Well, actually, most nights, now that I say it out loud, and before work stuff.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Work stuff — meetings, or something else?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Monday stand-ups, client meetings. I've got a part-time diploma as well, so exams too. I feel it in my throat beforehand. Then I walk in and I'm more or less fine.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any pain in the chest when the heart is going?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain. I'm twenty-four, doc, I'm not having a heart attack.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good, no chest pain. Do you get short of breath with it?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit, only a bit, at night and before an exam or a meeting. It's not like I can't breathe, I just notice it. She makes it sound worse.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you fainted, or felt you might pass out?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. I don't get dizzy either, and I drive just fine. I used to gym, but I haven't been in ages — Virgin Active by the office is hectic expensive.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): So no blackouts and no dizziness. You keep saying you're not stressed. How big a part do you think pressure is playing?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not stressed. Everyone wants to call it that, but work is work and the diploma is whatever. I handle it.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll leave the stress label alone for now. What about coffee, cold drinks, energy drinks?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Coffee, ja. Maybe four cups, sometimes five if the morning drags. And a Score in the afternoon, or a Monster, sometimes two. It's not that much.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Four or five coffees plus one or two energy drinks is a lot of caffeine in a day. Do you smoke, or vape?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I vape. I don't smoke cigarettes — I dropped those in matric. The vape is the mint nicotine one, pretty much all day. It's not the same as cigarettes.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Understood. Any medicines — inhalers, tablets from the chemist, anything regular?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): I've got the blue inhaler. The Ventolin, for my asthma. I puff it when I feel tight, maybe twice a week. And I was on the purple inhaler, but I stopped that.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): The purple one — what was it called, and when did you stop?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Seretide. The preventer. I stopped it round about last winter, because I felt fine. Don't ask me the dose, I never looked at the numbers on the thing.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ventolin when you need it, Seretide stopped since last winter, dose unknown. Anything else — Panado, vitamins, something someone gave you?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Panado, the odd one, if my head's sore. Oh, my flatmate tried to hand me his little white tablet, a beta blocker for his blood pressure. I didn't take it — not mine.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm glad you left his tablet alone. We'll ignore that completely. Any allergies — medicines, foods, anything?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. I can take whatever.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): No known allergies, then. Any operations?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Nope. Never been opened up. Appendix still in there, far as I know.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): And in the family — heart rhythm trouble, thyroid disease, anyone dying suddenly young?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): My ouma had a thyroid thing. She was on tablets for it. My dad's fine. Nobody dropped dead.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grandmother with a thyroid condition. The asthma — has that been with you a long time?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Since I was a kid, ja. It's mild. I don't even count it half the time. Doesn't stop me doing anything.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me have a look at you. Pulse is 104, blood pressure 128 over 76, oxygen sat 98 percent, respiratory rate 16.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): 104 is just because I'm in this chair. It'll settle. Watch.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): It might. Heart sounds are normal and there's no murmur, though it's ticking fast. Lungs are clear, no wheeze. Ankles aren't swollen.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): See? Nothing on me. Told you it was a waste of a gap.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): The exam is reassuring, yes. I still want the timing clear. Does this wake you, or is it while you're falling asleep?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Mostly while I'm falling asleep. I lie there listening to it. Sometimes it wakes me around two, and then I scroll my phone, which is probably stupid, hey.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the shortness of breath — same moments as the racing, or on its own?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): With it. Same time. In the parking lot before a meeting my chest goes tight and my heart's off, and then I'm inside and it's fine-ish. Embarrassing, not scary.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bowels, waterworks, skin — any of that bothering you?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): No. All good. I eat, I sleep, well, I sleep when my heart lets me. No rash, no funny urine.

[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back so we're on the same page. Most nights, and before exams or meetings, your heart races and you get a bit short of breath. A lot of coffee, energy drinks, all-day vaping, and mild asthma in the background. You don't want this called stress, and you've had no pain, no blackouts.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): When you line it up like that it sounds worse. It's really not that deep.

[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): I hear you. Caffeine and nicotine can push a heart like this, and so can an overactive thyroid or a rhythm disturbance. I'm not going to call it anxiety — I don't have grounds for that label — and I'm not saying the heart is damaged.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): So you don't actually know what it is.

[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): I won't conclude today. My leaning is that the stimulants are doing a large share of these palpitations, but I can't rule out a thyroid problem or an arrhythmia until we've looked.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): So, tests. Obviously. Do I have to starve? I've got a meeting at four and I already had coffee.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): No fasting for this. I'd like an ECG, we'll fit it in before you go if the room is free, and thyroid bloods — TSH and free T4.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Stickers on the chest, ja, I've seen that. And then you put me on some heart tablet?

[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not today. I don't want to start a heart tablet before we see the tracing. I do want the energy drinks cut right back, the coffee halved if you can, and the vape eased off. Even that will tell us something.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Halving coffee, maybe. I'm not promising I'll quit the vape. That thing is glued to my hand.

[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not asking you to quit today. When it starts up, try a slow breathing drill — in for four, hold for four, out for six. Do it in the car before the meeting instead of another Score.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Breathing exercises. My girlfriend will be thrilled, she does yoga. I think it's a bit silly, but I'll try it, whatever.

[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): Try it these next two weeks, and come back in two weeks so we can go through the ECG and the thyroid results. If the tracing is abnormal I'll phone you sooner — you won't sit on that for two weeks. I'll send both requests to reception now so you don't have to carry a form.

spec.situation: Young adult with palpitations and breathlessness, worse at night and before exams or work meetings; downplays stress, drinks a lot of coffee and energy drinks, vapes; friend or partner contributes. Doctor orders ECG and thyroid tests, discusses breathing exercises.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.

omissions.text: Palpitations are described as skipping beats and then hammering/pounding, not just racing.
Palpitations are felt in the throat beforehand.
Palpitations occur before exams as well as before work meetings/stand-ups.
Shortness of breath occurs with the palpitations and is not separate; patient says it is mild and 'not like I can't breathe'.
Episodes are mostly while falling asleep, and sometimes wake him around 2 a.m.
Denied near-syncope/feeling he might pass out ('Never') in addition to no fainting and no dizziness.
No family history of sudden young death ('Nobody dropped dead').
No family history of heart rhythm trouble was elicited/denied.
Ventolin use detail: he uses it when he feels tight.
Seretide was stopped around last winter because he felt fine; dose unknown because he never looked at the numbers.
Patient was offered a flatmate's white beta blocker tablet for blood pressure but did not take it.
Asthma is described as mild and not limiting activity ('doesn't stop me doing anything').
Doctor explicitly stated he is not diagnosing anxiety/stress today: 'I'm not going to call it anxiety — I don't have grounds for that label.'
Doctor also stated he is not saying the heart is damaged.
ECG was intended before he leaves if the room is free.
No fasting is required for the planned tests.
If the ECG tracing is abnormal, the doctor will phone him sooner rather than wait two weeks.

omissions.text: Family history of heart rhythm trouble was asked about and denied ('nobody dropped dead' was recorded for sudden young death, but family history of heart rhythm trouble being absent was not recorded).
Family history of thyroid disease was in the grandmother, who was on tablets for it.
Father reported as fine/no relevant history.
Patient denied smoking cigarettes currently and said he quit cigarettes in matric; current nicotine use is via vape only.
Ventolin was identified by brand name as the blue inhaler.
Patient said he did not take his flatmate's 'little white tablet,' a beta blocker for blood pressure; this non-use was discussed and should not be recorded as medication use.
Palpitations are felt 'in the throat' beforehand.
Palpitations are not every day, though now most nights; they also occur before work meetings/exams and he is more or less fine once he walks in.
Episodes are described as embarrassing rather than scary.
Sometimes the palpitations wake him around 2 a.m.
Sleep is affected: 'I sleep when my heart lets me.'
Chest tightness occurs in the parking lot before a meeting, together with the palpitations and mild shortness of breath, and improves once he is inside.
Denial of blackouts was explicitly stated ('never').
No bowel symptoms, no urinary symptoms, and no rash were recorded, but he also said he is otherwise eating normally.
Doctor stated he was not going to start a heart tablet before seeing the ECG tracing.
Follow-up was specifically to review both the ECG and thyroid results in two weeks.
